common_name: Jersey Knight American Holly (Rutgers Male Pollinator Holly)

planting.note: Plant container or balled-and-burlapped trees in late winter or spring in acidic, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; Jersey Knight is a male-only Rutgers selection grown strictly as a pollen source for female American holly cultivars, not for its own berries.

directions: Jersey Knight is a male-flowering American holly selection bred at Rutgers University specifically to serve as a reliable pollen source for female cultivars such as Jersey Princess and Dan Fenton, since American holly is dioecious and only pollinated female plants set berries. It grows into a dense, uniformly pyramidal evergreen tree with dark, semi-glossy spiny leaves, developing into a handsome screen or specimen tree in its own right even though it never produces fruit. Site one Jersey Knight within about 50 feet of several female American hollies to ensure consistent pollination and heavy berry crops each winter. Plant in acidic, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade and expect steady but moderate growth over its lifetime.
sources: Rutgers University New Jersey Agricultural Experiment Station

common_name: Maryland Dwarf American Holly (Prostrate Groundcover Native Holly)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in acidic, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; Maryland Dwarf is a naturally prostrate sport of American holly grown for its low, wide-spreading mounded form rather than for fruit or flowers.

directions: Maryland Dwarf is a naturally prostrate, low-mounding sport of American holly that spreads two to three times wider than it grows tall, making it a useful broadleaf evergreen groundcover or foundation shrub rather than a tree-form holly. Its small, dark, spiny leaves cover the plant densely from the ground up, and because flowering and fruiting are sparse on this selection it is grown chiefly for year-round textured foliage and form rather than for berries. Give it acidic, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade and allow ample horizontal room to spread, since shearing to control width sacrifices its naturally graceful mounded outline. It combines well with taller upright hollies as a low, tidy edging planting beneath windows or along foundations.

common_name: Miss Helen American Holly (Large Red-Fruited Pyramidal Native Holly)

planting.note: Plant container or balled-and-burlapped trees in late winter or spring in acidic, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; Miss Helen is a slow-growing female American holly selection valued for exceptionally large red berries on a refined pyramidal frame.

directions: Miss Helen is a female American holly selection prized for producing an unusually heavy set of large red berries against dense, refined pyramidal branching and glossy olive-green foliage. It grows slowly into a strong-leadered evergreen tree that holds its shape with little pruning, and under good conditions a single specimen can remain productive and attractive for decades. Because it is female, fruiting depends on a nearby male American holly such as Jersey Knight for pollination; without one nearby it will flower but set little or no fruit. Plant in acidic, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade and expect a refined specimen or screening tree well suited to Southern landscapes.

common_name: Dan Fenton American Holly (Rutgers Dark-Leaved Pyramidal Native Holly)

planting.note: Plant container or balled-and-burlapped trees in late winter or spring in acidic, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; Dan Fenton is a Rutgers female selection with dark, nearly rounded glossy leaves and a broadly conical form.

directions: Dan Fenton is a Rutgers University-selected female American holly named for a noted holly enthusiast credited with planting thousands of hollies, chosen for its exceptionally dark, glossy, nearly rounded leaves and broadly conical growth habit. It bears quarter-inch globose red berries in heavy quantity once pollinated by a nearby male American holly, and the fruit persists well into winter, drawing songbirds when other food sources have thinned. The dense, strongly pyramidal form and rich foliage color make it a striking specimen or screening tree distinct from lighter-leaved holly cultivars. Grow it in acidic, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade for the best foliage color and fruit set.
sources: Rutgers University New Jersey Agricultural Experiment Station

common_name: Satyr Hill American Holly (Holly Society 2003 Holly of the Year)

planting.note: Plant container or balled-and-burlapped trees in late winter or spring in acidic, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; Satyr Hill is a vigorous, open-pyramidal female American holly named 2003 Holly of the Year by the Holly Society of America for its heavy, well-spaced berry set.

directions: Satyr Hill is a vigorous female American holly selection named Holly of the Year by the Holly Society of America in 2003 for its consistently heavy crop of bright red, well-spaced berries that persist from early fall through winter. It grows into a large, upright, open-pyramidal evergreen tree that stays more loosely branched than many compact holly cultivars, giving it a naturally airy silhouette. Because it is a female clone, a male American holly must be planted nearby for reliable pollination and the heaviest berry crops. Plant in acidic, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade, and give it room to grow into a substantial specimen or wildlife tree over time.

common_name: Croonenburg American Holly (Self-Fruiting Perfect-Flowered Native Holly)

planting.note: Plant container or balled-and-burlapped trees in late winter or spring in acidic, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; Croonenburg is an unusual American holly with perfect (bisexual) flowers, so it sets berries reliably without a separate male pollinator nearby.

directions: Croonenburg is an unusual American holly selection that carries both functional male and female flower parts on the same plant, so unlike most dioecious holly cultivars it reliably sets a good crop of red berries without needing a separate pollinator nearby. Its leaves are noticeably less spiny than typical American holly, glossy dark green, and held on a dense, upright, pyramidal tree that eventually reaches substantial size. This self-fruiting habit makes Croonenburg a practical choice for smaller properties or single-tree plantings where there isn't room for both a male and female holly. Plant in acidic, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade and expect steady growth into a large, berry-laden specimen tree.
sources: Crape Myrtle Publishing Looking at Plants Database

common_name: Jewel Yaupon Holly (Heavy-Fruiting Open-Branched Native Holly)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; Jewel is a female yaupon holly selection grown for an unusually heavy annual crop of small red berries on an open, irregularly upright native shrub.

directions: Jewel is a female yaupon holly selection valued chiefly for its consistently heavy set of small red berries carried on an irregularly upright, open-branched native shrub. Like the species, it produces the tiny, finely toothed evergreen leaves typical of yaupon holly and tolerates the heat, drought, salt spray, and poor soils common along the Gulf Coast with ease. Because yaupon holly is dioecious, planting a male selection such as Will Fleming or the unselected species nearby ensures pollination and the heaviest possible berry crop each fall and winter. It responds well to light shaping but looks most natural left to develop its own loose, multi-stemmed form.
sources: University of Florida IFAS Gardening Solutions
